name: Nehemiah
author: Much of this book is the personal memoir of Nehemiah, a Jewish man living in exile who served as cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I. A cupbearer tasted and served the king's wine, a trusted post close to the throne. The king later appointed Nehemiah governor of Judah. Jewish tradition treats Ezra and Nehemiah as one book, possibly put together by Ezra, while many scholars think a later editor combined Nehemiah's memoir with other records and lists.
audience: It was first read by the small Jewish community in and around Jerusalem, descendants of exiles who had come back from Babylon, probably in the generation or so after Nehemiah. They were poor, few in number and surrounded by unfriendly neighbours, and their city's walls had been rebuilt within living memory.
era: Judah was a small province of the vast Persian Empire. The Babylonians had destroyed Jerusalem around 586 BC, and from around 538 BC Persian kings allowed Jewish exiles to return. The temple was rebuilt by around 516 BC, but the city walls remained broken. Nehemiah's work begins around 445 BC, in the reign of Artaxerxes I.

notes.1:1: Nehemiah is at Susa, a royal Persian capital, in the month of Kislev (November–December), around 445 BC.
notes.2:1: The month of Nisan (March–April) falls about four months after Nehemiah first heard the news from Jerusalem.
notes.2:9: Sanballat was governor of neighbouring Samaria, known also from ancient letters found in Egypt; Tobiah was an Ammonite official, and Geshem an Arab leader.
notes.5:14: Nehemiah served as governor for twelve years, from about 445 to 433 BC.
notes.6:15: The month of Elul falls in August–September, so the wall was finished in late summer, around 445 BC.
notes.7:6: This list closely matches one in Ezra. It records families who returned from exile, with Zerubbabel among their leaders, in the decades after 538 BC, nearly a century earlier.
notes.8:1: The seventh month (September–October) held Israel's major autumn festivals; scholars debate whether Ezra arrived in Jerusalem before Nehemiah, as traditionally held, or after.
notes.8:13: The Festival of Booths, or Tabernacles, was a week-long autumn harvest feast when families lived in shelters made of branches.
notes.12:1: These lists trace priestly families from the first return around 538 BC through several later generations of the Persian period.
notes.13:4: These events come after Nehemiah returned to the Persian king around 433 BC and later came back to Jerusalem.

flags.problem: The date of the book's final form is disputed. 'Probably in the generation or so after Nehemiah' gives only one view; many scholars place the final editing later, around 400 BC or into the Greek period. The claim that the walls had been rebuilt 'within living memory' depends on the earlier date but is stated as fact.
flags.suggestion: Add a short clause such as 'traditionally soon after Nehemiah's time, though many scholars think it reached its final form somewhat later'. Soften or drop 'within living memory'.

flags.problem: Ezra appears suddenly in a scholarly debate without being introduced. The author section mentions him only as a possible compiler, so readers may not know he was a priest and scribe who taught the law. Pairing the festival month with the dating debate in one sentence also makes the note hard to follow.
flags.suggestion: Briefly identify Ezra, for example 'Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law'. Consider splitting the festival detail and the Ezra–Nehemiah order debate into separate sentences.

unsure.problem: In 2:9 Nehemiah reaches the governors of the region with the king's letters. Sanballat and Tobiah are first named at 2:10, and Geshem not until 2:19. A reader on 2:9 will find these names explained a verse too early.
unsure.suggestion: Restored: notes cannot move. Word it for its passage. Original suggestion: Move this note to 2:10 and mention Geshem there or at 2:19. Alternatively, rewrite the 2:9 note about the king's letters and the regional governors.
